evidence.claim: A marsh channel and a former ferry port frame the shore.
evidence.quote: The Wachapreague Channel winds from the town, through the seaside marsh, out to the barrier islands.

evidence.claim: a former ferry port
evidence.quote: It is also known for the concrete ships sunk to protect the former ferry port from erosion during severe storms.

evidence.claim: On Virginia’s Eastern Shore, Route 13 divides the peninsula into bayside and seaside areas.
evidence.quote: The county is divided, as is the town, into bayside and seaside areas, which refer to the land on either side of the highway, Route 13 (Lankford Highway), which runs through Accomack and Northampton counties.

evidence.claim: Route 180 crosses between them, passing through Pungoteague and Keller before reaching Wachapreague’s waterfront in the Atlantic-side wetlands.
evidence.quote: SR 180 is a cross-peninsula highway in southern Accomack County that passes through Pungoteague and Keller

evidence.claim: At Wachapreague, the channel continues through marshes toward the barrier islands.
evidence.quote: The Wachapreague Channel winds from the town, through the seaside marsh, out to the barrier islands.

evidence.claim: At the peninsula’s southern end, Kiptopeke served as the northern landing for ferries across the lower Chesapeake Bay.
evidence.quote: By 1949, the Virginia Ferry Corporation owned the property, which it continued to use through 1964 as the northern terminus for the Little Creek-Cape Charles Ferry service which crossed the lower Chesapeake Bay

evidence.claim: The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel replaced that service in 1964.
evidence.quote: In 1964, the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel replaced the ferry

evidence.claim: The former terminal later became a campground, then a state park in 1992.
evidence.quote: Sometime after 1968, John Maddox purchased the ferry terminal and ran a campground there. Unable to get a loan to develop the land he agreed to sell it to state for $7.5 million, half of its appraised value, in 1992 so they could create a state park.

evidence.claim: For the drive to Wachapreague, Route 180 runs east from Pungoteague to Keller, briefly joins US 13 north, then turns east across an inactive railroad line.
evidence.quote: The state highway continues southeast and then east as Pungoteague Road to the town of Keller. SR 180 follows 1st Street to US 13 (Lankford Highway), then heads north along the U.S. Highway to the northern town limit of Keller. The state highway has a grade crossing of an inactive railroad line immediately to the east of US 13, then heads east as Wachapreague Road.

evidence.claim: Wachapreague Road becomes Main Street, ending at Atlantic Avenue beside the channel.
evidence.quote: SR 180 follows Main Street through the town of Wachapreague to its eastern terminus at SR 1701 (Atlantic Avenue) on the waterfront of a channel within the wetlands on the Atlantic Ocean side of the peninsula.

evidence.claim: A Virginia highway marker dates Onancock’s founding to 1680.
evidence.quote: According to a nearby Virginia state highway marker, Onancock was founded in 1680.

evidence.claim: In the mid-19th century, the town was a stagecoach stop between Wilmington, Delaware, and Eastville.
evidence.quote: In the mid-19th century, Onancock was a point along the stagecoach route between Wilmington, Delaware and Eastville, Virginia.

evidence.claim: Its creek had also brought a call for military aid: on November 28, 1782, Commodore Zedechiah Whaley sailed upstream and appealed to Lieutenant Colonel John Cropper.
evidence.quote: On November 28, 1782, he sailed up Onancock Creek and appealed to Lt. Colonel John Cropper

evidence.claim: Cropper gathered 25 local men, who boarded Whaley’s flagship, Protector, to join the campaign against British barges.
evidence.quote: who rounded up 25 local men in support.  They boarded Whaley's flagship, Protector, and continued his siege upon the British flotilla.

evidence.quote: SR 180 follows Main Street through the town of Wachapreague to its eastern terminus at SR 1701 (Atlantic Avenue) on the waterfront

evidence.claim: Beyond town, Wachapreague Channel winds through seaside marsh and reaches the Atlantic between Cedar and Parramore islands.
evidence.quote: The Wachapreague Channel winds from the town, through the seaside marsh, out to the barrier islands. Between Cedar and Parramore Islands it reaches the Atlantic Ocean.

evidence.claim: Access to both marsh and ocean draws fishermen here.
evidence.quote: Easy access to the marsh and ocean makes this a popular place for fishermen.

evidence.claim: The town’s name comes from the Wachapreague, an Algonquian people who lived in the area centuries ago.
evidence.quote: The name of the town came from the Wachapreague, an Algonquian people who resided in the area centuries ago.

evidence.claim: Wachapreague Channel winds from the waterfront into the seaside marsh.
evidence.quote: The Wachapreague Channel winds from the town, through the seaside marsh, out to the barrier islands.

evidence.quote: In 1964, the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel replaced the ferry

evidence.claim: John Maddox later bought the terminal and operated a campground before selling the property to the state in 1992.
evidence.quote: Sometime after 1968, John Maddox purchased the ferry terminal and ran a campground there. Unable to get a loan to develop the land he agreed to sell it to state for $7.5 million, half of its appraised value, in 1992 so they could create a state park.

evidence.claim: The terminal building became an education and concessions building, but was razed by 2002.
evidence.quote: The terminal building on the pier originally served as an education and concessions building, but by 2002 it was razed.

evidence.claim: The park’s shoreline, beach and piers give access to the Chesapeake Bay’s brackish water.
evidence.quote: The park offers recreational access to the brackish waters of the Chesapeake Bay with its shoreline, beach, boat ramps and piers

evidence.claim: In the Battle of Kedges Strait, Protector fought on after three other barges withdrew; 25 of its 65 men were killed or wounded.
evidence.quote: In what became the Battle of Kedges Strait three out of four of Whaley's barges turned back under heavy British fire, leaving the Protector alone to press on with the fight. Vastly outnumbered, ultimately 25 of its 65 men were killed or wounded

evidence.claim: The shoreline also provides migratory bird habitat along the East Coast flyway, another role for land once used to move motorists across the bay.

flags: PARTIAL OVERVIEW: cache/00.txt contains only the general Virginia Byway definition; its actual byway list is absent. The specific designation, 1994 date, Seaside Road alignment and connections to Accomac and Onancock cannot be reverified. Removed those current routing claims.

No cached designation-body account explains this corridor’s scenic merits. No end-to-end alignment, drive time or construction history is supported. Overview gives only the verified Route 180 approach and regional crossing history.
Moments run north to south, consistent with material’s Nassawadox-to-Kiptopeke mileage direction. Northern moments are outside that strip extract; coordinates establish their order.
Wachapreague is shorter than 90 words because the cache supplies little beyond the channel geography and name.
Dropped the current Onancock peace-treaty timing claim: the cache conflates treaty drafting with the 1782 action and offers no underlying historical document to resolve the distinction.
Kiptopeke ferry-start chronology differs between the community account (1954 US 13 relocation) and park account (property used by 1949); omitted the start date.
Onancock founding remains attributed to the Virginia highway marker. The combat account is retained in a measured register without the unverified treaty chronology or last-naval-action superlative.
